what.label: The Project
what.heading: Not a homestead. An engineered system.
what.body_1: Most self-sufficiency content does not show the real numbers. We do — including the corrections when they're wrong.
what.body_2: This is the documentation of an autonomous circular food system built on a Mediterranean finca: hydroponics, aquaponics, composting, solar, water architecture, sensor networks, and the food that comes out of all of it. The system produces approximately 71% of the calories and 90% of the protein two adults need. The remainder is rice.
what.body_3: Every calculation is published. Every error is corrected in public. The system is live data.

thesis.body: Intelligent people who think rigorously about almost everything have almost nowhere rigorous to go when they want to understand food. The calorie maths is never done. The errors are never corrected. The calculations are never shown. This project exists because that gap is real and because closing it is an engineering problem, not an identity statement.

subscribe.preview_heading: The planning framework: why self-sufficiency calculations usually fail
subscribe.preview_body_1: The first question anyone serious about food autonomy asks is: how many calories does a system need to produce? The second question — which almost no one asks — is: how do you verify that number? The gap between those two questions is where almost every self-sufficiency project fails.
subscribe.preview_body_2: Our original projection placed caloric self-sufficiency at 85–95%. This was not a guess — it was built from a detailed system model with planting schedules, yield tables, and nutritional data. It was also wrong. A subsequent material flow audit found three compounding errors that reduced the figure to 45–55%.
subscribe.preview_body_3: The errors were not random. They followed a pattern that appears in almost every self-sufficiency calculation we have reviewed: optimistic yield assumptions, missing loss factors, and a systematic underestimation of caloric density requirements under physical work conditions. Each error is small. Compounded, they produce projections that bear no relationship to what a system will actually produce.
subscribe.preview_body_4: This issue documents the correction methodology: how the audit was structured, what each error source was, and how the system was redesigned to reach the current figure of 71%. The methodology is transferable. You can apply it to any system design, including one at your own scale.
